# Where this is going {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
Quick framing before I start. This is a walkthrough, not a pitch — I want you to
leave knowing enough about the internals to decide whether it fits your pipeline,
and to debug it when it doesn't. I'll stop at five points to jump into RStudio and
run things live, so shout if you want me to try something specific on the way
through.
:::

## The one-sentence version

> Give it a character vector of messy free-text Australian addresses.
> Get back the best-matching **G-NAF record**, its **coordinates**, and a
> **transparent 0–100 confidence score broken down by component** — for a few rows
> or a few million.

::: {.fragment}
```r
results <- gnaf_match(dt$address_string, con)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
That is the whole API surface for the common case. Everything else in this deck is
about what happens *inside* that call, and which knobs matter for **your** use case.
:::

::: {.notes}
If you take one slide away, take this one. The interface is deliberately boring:
a character vector in, a data.table out, one row per match. No per-address loop,
no REST calls, no service to stand up, no API key.

The reason I am doing forty slides about a one-line API is that the defaults are
tuned for a middle-of-the-road use case, and I know at least two teams in this room
are not middle-of-the-road.
:::

## Why we keep rebuilding this

Real address data is human-typed:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `RD` vs `ROAD` vs `Rd.`
- `MT GRAVATT` vs `MOUNT GRAVATT EAST`
- Unit numbers in four notations: `U110`, `110/120`, `UNIT 110 120`, `110 120`
- Building names where the street number should be
- Postcodes off by a digit — or absent
- Suburbs spelt phonetically
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
An exact string join to G-NAF fails on a large fraction of real input.

A naive fuzzy join over 15M rows does not finish.

The interesting work is in the middle: **block cheaply, score honestly, fall back
deliberately.**
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Everyone here who has done address matching has written some version of this.
The failure mode is always the same: the exact join gets you 60 to 70 percent and
then you spend three weeks on the tail.

The point I want to land is that the hard part is not the string similarity metric.
Jaro-Winkler is one function call. The hard part is candidate generation: how you
get from fifteen million rows down to the twenty you are willing to score, without
throwing away the right answer on the way. That is what most of match.R is.
:::

## Two audiences in this room

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### [High precision]{.precision}

"I need to know **this exact dwelling**."

- Unit-level correctness matters
- A wrong match is worse than no match
- Downstream: record linkage, service delivery, counts by address
- Wants: high `min_score`, flat weight up, alias resolution, a review queue
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### [Normalisation]{.normalise}

"I need a **clean consistent string** — and roughly the right spot."

- Street or suburb level is fine
- Coverage matters more than precision
- Downstream: dedupe, aggregation, mapping, tidy display
- Wants: low `min_score`, street-only fallback, aliases on, `address_label` as the output
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
gnafr is **one engine with different settings**, not two packages. I will flag
[precision]{.precision} / [normalisation]{.normalise} implications as we go, and put
both recipes side by side at the end.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the thread through the whole deck, so I want it explicit up front.

Some of you are doing high-precision work where a wrong unit number is a real error
with consequences. Others are doing normalisation, where you mostly want the messy
string turned into something canonical, and being one house number off is annoying
but survivable.

The design decision I made — and the one I most want feedback on today — is that
these should be the same code path with different arguments, not two modes. The
reason is the score breakdown: if you can see which component agreed, you can set
your own bar. A single opaque confidence number would have forced me to pick a
philosophy on your behalf.
:::

## What is G-NAF, quickly

The **Geocoded National Address File** — Australia's authoritative address dataset,
published by Geoscape. Around 15M records, each with a persistent identifier,
structured components, and a geocoded lat/long.

| Format | What it is | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Core CSV** | One flattened, simplified CSV per state | Default. Smaller, simpler. |
| **Standard PSV** | The raw product: dozens of pipe-delimited tables (`ADDRESS_DETAIL`, `ADDRESS_ALIAS`, `STREET_LOCALITY_ALIAS`, `LOCALITY_ALIAS`, …) | When you want the **official alias records** and the full column set |

::: {.fragment}
gnafr loads either — `gnaf_load()` for Core CSV, `gnaf_load_psv()` for raw PSV.
**Use the PSV if you can**: you get official suburb/street synonyms, mesh block
codes, primary/secondary dwelling linkage, and geocode reliability type.
:::

::: {.notes}
Some of you already have G-NAF loaded somewhere — a SQL Server table, Postgres, a
folder of CSVs. This is not asking you to change your source of truth; it builds a
local, query-optimised copy.

The Core versus Standard distinction matters more than people expect. Core is what
most pipelines use because it is one file. But the alias tables in the Standard
product are the single biggest coverage win available: about a quarter of the rows
in my loaded database are alias rows. I will come back to that in detail.
:::

## The package, in layers

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '15px'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  subgraph BUILD["One-off build"]
    direction TB
    L1["G-NAF Core CSV<br/>or Standard PSV"] --> L2["gnaf_load()<br/>gnaf_load_psv()"]
    L2 --> L3[("gnaf.duckdb<br/>persists on disk")]
    L3 --> L4["gnaf_build_street_aliases()<br/>gnaf_rebuild_locality_index()"]
    L4 --> L3
  end

  subgraph RUN["Every run"]
    direction TB
    R1["character vector<br/>of addresses"] --> R2["address_parse()"]
    R2 --> R3["gnaf_match()<br/>score + rank + fall back<br/><i>inside DuckDB</i>"]
    R3 --> R4["data.table:<br/>scores, coords, PIDs"]
  end

  L3 -.-> R3
  R4 --> S1["spatial_lookup()<br/>plot_boundaries_heatmap()"]
  R4 --> S2["gnaf_app()<br/>Shiny review"]
```

::: {.notes}
Two phases. The build is a one-off measured in minutes, and the artefact is a
single DuckDB file you can copy onto a network drive and share read-only across a
team. The run phase never re-reads the source data.

Note the dotted line: matching queries the database directly. The address table
never comes into R memory. That is the whole reason this scales, and I will unpack
it properly when I get to the DuckDB slide.
:::

| `parse.R` | Free text into structured components (`address_parse`) | 1,338 |

::: {.notes}
I am showing this because this audience will want to read the source, and it is
worth knowing where the weight sits. Parsing and matching are three thousand of the
six thousand three hundred lines, and that ratio is about right — those are the two
places real-world messiness actually lives.

The one worth a second look is score.R being small. The scoring rules are
deliberately simple; all the sophistication is in deciding which pairs get scored
at all.
:::

# Part 1 — Building the database {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
Four parts: build, parse, score, match. Then the extras — aliases, cache,
performance, spatial, the app — and then the two recipes.

Part one is the shortest, because it is the part you do once.
:::

## Setup is a one-off

```r
library(gnafr)

con <- gnaf_connect("C:/temp/gnaf.duckdb")

gnaf_build_db(
  con,
  gnaf_dir = "C:/temp/gnaf/G-NAF/G-NAF MAY 2026/Standard",
  states   = "QLD"          # a single code, c("QLD","NSW"), or "all"
)

gnaf_status(con)
#>              table    rows
#>     gnaf_addresses 3305035
#>   custom_addresses       0
```

::: {.fragment}
`gnaf_build_db()` is a wrapper that runs, in order:

1. `gnaf_init()` — create tables, indexes, run any schema migrations
2. `gnaf_load_psv()` — read the raw PSV files straight into DuckDB
3. `gnaf_build_street_aliases()` — derive number-free street records
:::

::: {.notes}
Three lines to a match-ready database. The file persists — you never call init or
load again, you just reconnect.

The states argument takes a vector, or the string "all", which detects whichever
state files you actually downloaded. And overwrite equals TRUE only clears the
states you are reloading, so you can refresh Queensland without disturbing New
South Wales.

Worth saying out loud: DuckDB reads the PSV files itself. The data does not pass
through R. On my laptop, Queensland is a couple of minutes.
:::

## What `gnaf_init()` actually creates

Two structurally identical tables — `gnaf_addresses` and `custom_addresses` — plus:

| Object | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `idx_gnaf_pc` | Index on `postcode` — supports the state and locality paths |
| `idx_gnaf_pcnum` | Compound `(postcode, number_first)` — **the index the hot path relies on** |
| `idx_gnaf_label` | Index on `address_label` — backs the exact-label fast path |
| `gnaf_locality_index` | Deduplicated `(locality_name, postcode, state)` — about 3,000 rows per state |
| `gnaf_match_cache` | `input_standardised` → PID plus all six score components |

::: {.fragment}
Every statement is `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` / `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, so
`gnaf_init()` is always safe to re-run — including on a database built by an older
version of the package.
:::

::: {.notes}
The compound postcode-plus-number index is the one that matters. It is what makes
the primary matching path an indexed equi-join rather than a scan.

The locality index deserves a mention because it is a small design decision with a
big payoff. When the postcode is wrong, I need a fuzzy scan over suburb names.
Doing that against three million address rows is expensive; doing it against a
deduplicated three thousand row lookup is basically free. It gets rebuilt whenever
you load, and you can force it with gnaf_rebuild_locality_index.
:::

## Every column comes along

Not just the fields needed for string matching:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `address_detail_pid` — the persistent G-NAF ID
- `address_label` — the canonical formatted string
- `longitude` / `latitude`
- `mb_code` — ABS Mesh Block
- `legal_parcel_id` — cadastral lot/plan
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `geocode_type` — e.g. `PROPERTY CENTROID`
- `alias_principal` / `principal_pid`
- `primary_secondary` / `primary_pid`
- `address_site_name`
- `date_created`
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Precision work]{.precision}: `primary_secondary` and `geocode_type` are how you tell
"the building" from "unit 4 in the building", and how you tell a surveyed point from
a street-centreline approximation.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is one of the reasons to prefer the PSV loader. The Core CSV drops a lot of
this.

Geocode type in particular is underused. A property-centroid geocode and a
street-locality-centroid geocode are wildly different in accuracy, and if you are
doing anything spatial downstream — catchment assignment, distance calculations —
you want to filter or at least flag on it. gnafr does not do that for you, but it
hands you the column.
:::

## Reconnecting later

```r
library(gnafr)
con <- gnaf_connect("C:/temp/gnaf.duckdb")

# Multiple R processes reading the same file at once:
con <- gnaf_connect("C:/temp/gnaf.duckdb", read_only = TRUE)
```

::: {.fragment}
Keep **one connection open** across many `gnaf_match()` calls — reconnecting per
call is measurably slower. In Shiny or a service, hold it at module level.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## DuckDB storage format
If you upgrade the `duckdb` package across a storage-format change, the file must be
rebuilt. Pin `duckdb` in production, or keep the build script handy.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The read-only flag is how a team shares one database. Put the file on a network
drive, everyone connects read-only, no locking problems. One caveat: the match cache
can still be read, but writes are silently skipped on a read-only connection — so a
shared copy only benefits from whatever was cached when it was built. That is by
design, not an error; the write is caught and swallowed.

The DuckDB version thing has bitten me. It is not corruption; it is a deliberate
refusal to open a file written by a different storage format. Rebuild and move on.
:::

# Part 2 — Parsing {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
This is the part I would most like technical feedback on, because it is where the
Australian-specific knowledge is baked in, and several of you have probably solved
the same problems differently.
:::

## `address_parse()` — free text to fields

```r
address_parse(c(
  "unit 110 120 musgrave Road red hill 4000 QLD",
  "Cambridge on the hill 110/120 musgrave road red hill QLD 4000"
))
```

```
   input_id in_postcode in_state in_locality in_street_name in_street_type
1      4000         QLD  RED HILL       MUSGRAVE           ROAD
2      4000         QLD  RED HILL       MUSGRAVE           ROAD

   in_number_first in_flat_type in_flat_number in_building_name
1              120         UNIT            110               NA
2              120         UNIT            110   CAMBRIDGE ON THE HILL
```

::: {.fragment}
Standalone and database-free. Use it for **data profiling and debugging** before you
match anything.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is exported deliberately. When a match looks wrong, this is always the first
thing to run — nine times out of ten the parse explains it, and you have not learned
anything by staring at the score.

Full field list: postcode, state, locality, street name, street type, street suffix,
number first, number last, number suffix, flat type, flat number, building name.
:::

## The parse pipeline

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '15px'}}}%%
flowchart TB
  A["Raw string"] --> B["Uppercase, trim,<br/>collapse whitespace"]
  B --> C["Strip trailing postcode + state<br/><i>either order</i>"]
  C --> D{"Comma present?"}
  D -- yes --> E["Token before the LAST comma<br/>is a strong street-type hint<br/><i>fuzzy, Jaro-Winkler</i>"]
  D -- no --> F["Rightmost street-type token"]
  E --> G["Anchor found"]
  F --> G
  G --> H{"Matches a<br/>vectorised fast path?"}
  H -- "yes (~95%)" --> I["4a slash · 4b flat-prefix<br/>4b2 attached letter · 4c simple"]
  H -- no --> J[".parse_single()<br/>row-by-row fallback"]
  I --> K["Normalise abbreviations"]
  J --> K
  K --> L["Structured components"]
```

::: {.notes}
Two tiers, and the split is a performance decision, not a correctness one.

Tier one is four stringi regex patterns applied across the entire input vector at
once. They cover about 95 percent of well-formed Australian addresses. Tier two is
a row-by-row fallback for everything else — misspelt street types, unusual
structures, addresses with no identifiable type at all.

If your data is dominated by tier two, matching will be slower. Profiling with
address_parse first tells you that before you commit to a big run.
:::

## The comma hint

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why the last comma matters
`"123 St James Rode, Tamborine Mountain QLD 4272"`

A plain rightmost-token scan finds `St` inside `St James` and calls it `STREET` —
hiding the real, misspelt type `Rode`.

The token before the **last comma** is checked against the known type list
**fuzzily** (Jaro-Winkler), so `RODE` resolves to `ROAD`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two failure modes fixed at once:

1. **Coincidental abbreviation collisions** inside multi-word street names
2. **Misspelt types** a pure rightmost scan would miss entirely
:::

::: {.notes}
This is my favourite bit of the parser, because it is a case where the punctuation
people leave in their data is actually informative rather than noise.

Most cleaning pipelines strip commas first thing. This one uses the last comma as a
structural signal: in Australian convention it separates the street part from the
locality part, so the token immediately before it is almost always the street type.

For the normalisation crowd — if you are pre-stripping punctuation before you hand
data to gnafr, stop. You are throwing away a signal it uses.
:::

## The four fast paths

| Path | Shape | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **4a** | `FLAT/NUMBER STREET` | `110/120 Musgrave Rd` |
| **4b** | `TYPE N N STREET` | `Unit 3 120 Musgrave Rd` |
| **4b2** | attached single letter | `F8 536 …`  (`F`=Flat, `A`=Apartment, `U`=Unit; anything else defaults to Unit) |
| **4c** | `NUMBER[-NUMBER] STREET` | `18-20 Drift Cl` — plus the *implied pair* sub-case |

::: {.fragment}
The **implied pair** is the one to know: `"10 120 Musgrave Rd"` — two bare numbers,
no `UNIT` keyword. Australian convention says that is unit 10 at number 120, and the
parser reads it that way.
:::

::: {.notes}
Implied pair is the one that surprises people, and it is worth a discussion.

Two bare numbers in a row is genuinely ambiguous — it could be unit ten at one
twenty, or it could be a typo, or a range written without the dash. The parser
commits to the Australian convention because that is overwhelmingly what it means
in practice.

If your data source is one where that assumption is wrong, tell me, because that is
exactly the sort of thing worth making configurable.
:::

## Flat, level, and lot are separate fields

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Flat prefixes recognised**

`UNIT`, `U` (attached, `U12`), `APARTMENT`, `APT`, `FLAT`, `FL`, `FLT`, `SUITE`,
`STE`, `SHOP`, `SH`, `VILLA`, `VLA`, `TENANCY`, `TNY`
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Parsed into their own fields**

`LEVEL`, `LVL`, `FLOOR`, `FLR` → `level_type` / `level_number`

`LOT` → `lot_number`
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
```r
address_parse("level 5 300 ann st brisbane 4000")
#> level_type = LEVEL, level_number = 5, number_first = 300
```
Level and lot are **not** folded into the flat component — a level 5 office and unit
5 are different things.
:::

::: {.notes}
Earlier versions did fold level into flat, and it caused a specific bug class:
"level 5, 300 Ann Street" matching "unit 5, 300 Ann Street" at full confidence.
In a CBD office tower those are completely different tenancies.

Lot numbers are stored and parsed, and lot-to-lot matching earns number credit, but
lot addressing in general — the "Lot 5 DP 12345" rural style — is not something I
would claim this handles well.
:::

## Normalisation (`normalize = TRUE`)

Applied to `in_locality` and `in_street_name` **after** structural parsing:

| Pattern | Expands to |
|---|---|
| `MNT`, `MT` | `MOUNT` |
| `ST` (whole word, after the street type is already extracted) | `SAINT` |
| `NTH`, `STH`, leading `N`/`S`/`E`/`W` | `NORTH` / `SOUTH` / `EAST` / `WEST` |
| `CK` | `CREEK` |
| `&` | `AND` |
| Ordinals `1ST`…`20TH` | `FIRST`…`TWENTIETH` (street name only) |

::: {.fragment}
`MT GRAVATT EAST` would still *score* well on Jaro-Winkler similarity. Expanding it
first turns a near-miss into a **perfect** component score — which matters when you
are thresholding at 90.
:::

::: {.notes}
Order matters here and it is easy to get wrong. ST is expanded to SAINT only after
the street type has been pulled out, otherwise every Smith Street becomes Smith
Saint.

The reason to bother at all, when Jaro-Winkler would have scored it in the high
nineties anyway: those small deficits accumulate. Lose a bit on suburb, lose a bit
on street name, and a genuinely correct match lands at 88 instead of 100 — below the
fallback threshold, so you pay for an extra query pass, and possibly below a
precision team's cutoff.
:::

## What the parser will not do

- **PO Box / GPO Box / Locked Bag** — no street component to anchor on
- **Rural lot addressing** (`Lot 5 DP 12345`) — lot numbers are stored, but this style is not matched
- **Non-standard street types** absent from the lookup table — the address still matches, but `score_street_type` is 0

::: {.fragment}
The full official type table lives in `inst/extdata/street_types.csv`. If your data
has a local abbreviation that is missing, **add it there** — that is the intended
extension point.
:::

::: {.notes}
Be honest about limits. PO boxes are the big one: if a meaningful share of your
input is postal addresses, filter them out before matching rather than letting them
come back unmatched and pollute your rate.

The street types CSV being a data file, not hard-coded, is deliberate. If someone
here has a corpus with local abbreviations I have not seen, send them to me and I
will add them upstream.
:::

```r
  "unit 110 120 musgrave Road red hill 4000 QLD",
  "U110 1120 musgrave rd red hill 4000",
  "Cambridge on the hill 110/120 musgrave road red hill QLD 4000",
  "18-20 drift cl goldsborough QLD 4865",
  "F8 536 example parade brisbane 4000",
  "123 St James Rode, Tamborine Mountain QLD 4272",
  "level 5 300 ann st brisbane 4000",
  "lot 7 kreis rd westbrook QLD 4350"
))

address_parse("Mt Gravatt East", normalize = TRUE)[, .(in_locality)]
address_parse("Mt Gravatt East", normalize = FALSE)[, .(in_locality)]
```

::: {.notes}
This is the best demo in the deck — take audience suggestions here. Ask people to
call out a genuinely horrible address from their own data and parse it live.

Have the normalize TRUE versus FALSE comparison ready as a fallback if nobody offers
anything. And if a suggestion parses badly, do not skip past it — that is the most
useful thing that can happen in this session.
:::

# Part 3 — Scoring {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
Now the bit everyone actually argues about. I want to be very concrete, because
"confidence score" means nothing until you know what is in it.
:::

## Six components, one total

```
total_score = score_postcode + score_suburb + score_street_name
            + score_street_type + score_number + score_flat
```

| Component | Default weight | How it is computed |
|---|---|---|
| `postcode` | **20** | Exact, with near-miss partial credit |
| `suburb` | **15** | `round(15 × jaro_winkler(input, candidate))` |
| `street_name` | **40** | `round(40 × jaro_winkler(input, candidate))` |
| `street_type` | **10** | Three-tier exact comparison |
| `number` | **10** | Exact / in-range / none |
| `flat` | **5** | Composite flat + level identifier |

::: {.fragment}
Street name carries the largest single weight — it is the strongest discriminator
between genuinely different addresses that share a postcode and a house number.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every one of these numbers came out of the source, not out of a slide I wrote from
memory.

The weighting philosophy: postcode and street name together are sixty of the
hundred, because those two agreeing is most of the evidence. Flat is only five,
which is the single most contentious choice in the package and the one the precision
people in the room should push back on. I will show you how to change it.
:::

## Postcode (20) — the only component with near-miss credit

::: {.spec}
Exact → **20**  ·  off by 1 → **14** (70%)  ·  by 2 → **8** (40%)  ·  by 3 → **4** (20%)  ·  further → **0**
:::

::: {.fragment}
But: the **primary path joins on `g.postcode = i.in_postcode`**. By construction,
every row it scores already has full postcode credit.

The partial-credit branches only become reachable on the **locality fallback**,
which widens the join to nearby postcodes (±3) or to whatever postcode a fuzzy
suburb match points at.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```r
# 4058 typed, 4059 correct — number and street match exactly, so the
# locality fallback finds it and awards 14 instead of rejecting it.
gnaf_match("10 Musgrave Road, Red Hill QLD 4058", con)[
  , .(matched, total_score, score_postcode, address_label)]
```
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a good example of scoring rules and candidate generation being tangled
together, which is the thing people get wrong when they read scoring code in
isolation.

You can read the near-miss branches in score.R and assume near-miss postcodes are
routinely retrieved. They are not. The primary path is a strict equi-join. Those
branches are dead code until the locality fallback widens the net — and that only
fires when the best score so far is at or below ninety.
:::

## Suburb (15) and street name (40)

Both are `round(weight × jaro_winkler_similarity(input, candidate))`.

::: {.fragment}
Computed by **DuckDB's built-in `jaro_winkler_similarity()`** for every path except
the exact-label fast path, which uses `stringdist::stringdist(method = "jw", p = 0.1)`
in R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Same metric — evaluated on whichever side of the SQL/R boundary that path happens to
run on.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters for reproducibility
Two implementations of one formula is a maintenance risk. It is deliberate — the
exact-label path never touches the join machinery, so it scores in R — but it is the
first place to look if a score ever disagrees with itself.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
For the technical crowd: the scoring logic genuinely exists twice in the source.
Once as generated DuckDB SQL CASE expressions, once as data.table vector operations.
They are kept in step by the test suite.

If I were starting again I would probably push everything through SQL and drop the R
copy, but the exact-label path is fast precisely because it avoids the join, so it
earns its exception.
:::

## Street type (10) — not a similarity score

::: {.spec}
Both agree, or both absent → **10**  ·  exactly one side has a type → **5**  ·  both have a type but they disagree → **4**
:::

Abbreviations are already canonicalised at parse time *and* at load time, so by the
time scoring runs "same type" should mean **string-equal**, not merely similar.

| Abbreviations | Canonical |
|---|---|
| `RD`, `RDS` | `ROAD` |
| `ST`, `STR` | `STREET` |
| `CT`, `CRT` | `COURT` |
| `CCT` | `CIRCUIT` |
| `TCE`, `TER`, `TERR` | `TERRACE` |

::: {.fragment}
The **40% floor for disagreement** is deliberate: typing `Avenue` where G-NAF has
`Drive` is a common, low-stakes user error and should not cancel out an otherwise
strong match.
:::

::: {.notes}
Note the asymmetry, because it is counter-intuitive: a missing street type scores
five out of ten, and a wrong street type scores four. Missing beats wrong, but only
just.

The reasoning is that people omit the type constantly and get it wrong occasionally,
and neither should be fatal when the number, street name and postcode all agree.

If you disagree with that four, it is a weight away from being whatever you want.
:::

## Street number (10) — and the gate

::: {.spec}
Exact match to `number_first` → **10**  ·  within `number_first`–`number_last` → **7**  ·  no match → **0**
:::

A parsed **suffix** (`190A`) is layered on top: it only earns credit when the
candidate's `address_label` literally starts with `"190A "` — so `190A` never matches
`190B` just because they share a numeric prefix.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## The number filter is a gate, not a soft score
In most paths, candidates whose number fails the pre-filter are **excluded from the
join entirely** and never reach scoring.

An input with a house number that is not in G-NAF for that street comes back
`matched = FALSE`, `match_status = "no_candidate"` — **not** a low-scoring row you
can rescue by lowering `min_score`.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the single most important slide for anyone debugging an unmatched address,
so do not rush it.

The intuition people bring is that every component is a soft score and lowering the
threshold surfaces more. That is true for five of the six components. It is not
true for number, because number is used as a pre-filter to keep the joined table
small — that is the performance trade.

So if you set min score to zero and something still does not match, the number gate
is the usual culprit. The escape hatch is the street-only fallback, which I will get
to.
:::

## Flat / level (5) — composite

::: {.spec}
Both sides have no flat, or identifiers match with no conflicting type → **5**
·  identifiers match but the supplied types conflict → **2** (50%)  ·  otherwise → **0**
:::

::: {.fragment}
A flat number on the input that the candidate does not have **at all** is treated as
a mismatch, not a "cannot tell" — a different unit at the same street number is a
meaningfully different physical address.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Precision teams]{.precision}: five points out of a hundred means a **completely wrong
unit** costs you a drop from 100 to 95. If unit-level correctness is your job,
either raise the flat weight or filter on `score_flat == 5` explicitly.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide where I expect an argument, and I want the argument.

The default of five reflects the median use case: most inputs do not have a unit
number at all, and weighting it heavily would punish every house address.

But for a precision workflow it is arguably wrong. A match at 95 that has the wrong
unit looks excellent on total score and is a real error. Two options: raise the
weight, or ignore total score for that check and filter on score flat directly. I
lean towards the filter, because it is explicit and it does not disturb the cache.
:::

## Rebalancing the weights

```r
results <- gnaf_match(
  addresses, con,
  weights = list(
    postcode    = 20,
    suburb      = 18,
    street_name = 25,
    street_type = 10,
    number      = 20,   # numbers matter more than postcode here
    flat        =  7
  )
)
```

Must be a **named list summing to 100**.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-important}
## Custom weights disable the match cache for that call
Cached scores were computed under the default weights. Reusing them under different
weights would silently misreport, so gnafr bypasses the cache entirely rather than
mix them.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Full control, with one consequence worth planning around.

If you run a nightly job with custom weights, you get no cache benefit ever, and
your cache tables stay empty. That is expected, not a bug — but it means the
performance numbers I show later do not apply to you.

My advice: settle on one weight set per pipeline and stick to it. If your custom
weights are stable and you want caching, tell me and I will key the cache on a
weight hash. It is not hard, I just have not needed it.
:::

## Reading the scores

| Range | Typical meaning |
|---|---|
| **90–100** | Near-certain. All components agree. |
| **75–89** | High confidence; minor spelling variation in suburb or street |
| **60–74** | Reasonable; one significant discrepancy |
| **40–59** | Low confidence — review manually |
| **< 60** | Filtered out by default (`min_score = 60`) |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Precision]{.precision}: `min_score = 90`, and inspect components — a strong total
built from postcode plus a lucky number match is not the same as one built from
street name.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Normalisation]{.normalise}: `min_score = 40` with `street_only_fallback = TRUE`.
A right-street, wrong-number match is a perfectly good normalisation result.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
These bands are guidance, not law. Calibrate on your own labelled data — the
distribution depends heavily on how messy your source is.

The point of the two-column split is that the same run can serve both teams. Match
once at a low threshold, keep every row, and let each downstream consumer apply its
own bar. You do not need two pipelines, and you do not want to re-run matching just
to change a cutoff.
:::

## {background-color="#0b3d5c"}

### Live demo 3 — score components, one at a time {.dim}

```r
# Wrong street type: Avenue typed, Drive in G-NAF
gnaf_match("13 Fairway Avenue, Clear Island Waters QLD 4226",
           con, min_score = 0)[, .(total_score, score_street_type, address_label)]

# Number inside a G-NAF range record (13-27)
gnaf_match("15 Fairway Drive, Clear Island Waters QLD 4226",
           con)[, .(total_score, score_number, address_label)]

# The gate: a number that is simply not in G-NAF
gnaf_match("999 Musgrave Road, Red Hill QLD 4059",
           con, min_score = 0)[, .(matched, match_status, total_score)]

# Full breakdown for one input
gnaf_match("unit 110 120 musgrave Road red hill 4000 QLD",
           con, max_results = 5, min_score = 20)
```

::: {.notes}
Walk these one at a time and read the numbers out loud against the rules from the
last few slides.

The third one is the money shot: min score zero and it still comes back unmatched.
That is the gate, made visible. Pause there and make sure everyone has it.
:::

# Part 4 — The matching cascade {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
Everything so far has been about a single input-candidate pair. This part is about
which candidates get generated in the first place — the part I said earlier is the
actual hard problem.
:::

## Six paths, tried in order

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '14px'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["gnaf_match(addresses)"] --> B{"Exact label<br/>match?"}
  B -- yes --> Z["Result"]
  B -- no --> C{"In match<br/>cache?"}
  C -- yes --> Z
  C -- no --> D["address_parse()"]
  D --> E{"Postcode<br/>parsed?"}
  E -- yes --> F["3 · Postcode path<br/><i>equi-join, hot path</i>"]
  E -- no --> G["4 · State path<br/><i>state-wide scan</i>"]
  F --> H{"Best score ≤<br/>fallback_threshold<br/>or unmatched?"}
  G --> H
  H -- no --> Z
  H -- "yes, locality parsed" --> I["5 · Locality fallback<br/>fuzzy suburb → postcode"]
  I --> J{"Still unmatched and<br/>street_only_fallback?"}
  J -- no --> Z
  J -- yes --> K["6 · Street-only fallback"]
  K --> Z
```

::: {.notes}
This is the central diagram of the whole talk. Everything else is detail hanging
off it.

The shape to notice: it is a cascade, and each input drops out as soon as it is
satisfied. In a typical batch the vast majority never get past path three. The
expensive paths — locality, street-only — only ever run on the residue.

That is also why the timing is nonlinear in your data quality rather than your row
count. A hundred thousand clean addresses are much faster than ten thousand awful
ones.
:::

## 1. Exact label match

If the uppercased, trimmed input equals a G-NAF `address_label` exactly, it is scored
and returned immediately — no parse-driven join at all.

::: {.fragment}
Built for **re-processing addresses that gnafr (or G-NAF) already standardised**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Implemented as a **hash join against a registered temporary table**, not a giant
SQL `IN (...)` list — so it stays fast at tens of thousands of inputs.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Normalisation workflows]{.normalise}: this is why round-tripping is cheap. Emit
`address_label`, feed it back next month, and it comes straight down this path.
:::

::: {.notes}
The registered-temp-table detail is worth calling out to this audience because it is
a trap people fall into. The obvious implementation is to build a huge IN list of
literals. That works at a hundred and dies at fifty thousand — the SQL parser itself
becomes the bottleneck.

duckdb_register lets DuckDB hash-join directly against an R data.table. Same idea as
a temp table, none of the round-trip cost.
:::

## 2. The match cache

`gnaf_match_cache` stores `input_standardised → (address_detail_pid, six scores)` for
every result that scored at or above `cache_threshold` (default **95**).

::: {.fragment}
Lookups join on `input_standardised` — the building/flat/number/street/locality string
gnafr derives from the **parsed** input. So a *differently worded but equivalently
parsed* address still hits the cache.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```r
"unit 110 120 musgrave rd red hill 4000"   # cached last month
"U110 120 Musgrave Road, RED HILL QLD 4000"  # different string, same parse → hit
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Only consulted and written when `weights` are exactly the package defaults.

Every entry is stamped with an **algorithm version**, and lookups filter on the
current one — so a scoring or parser change invalidates stale entries automatically
rather than silently serving them.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is my favourite optimisation in the package because it is cheap and it
compounds.

Keying on the standardised parse rather than the raw string is what makes it more
than a memoised lookup. Two records that a human would call the same address, written
differently, collapse to the same key. In administrative data where the same address
arrives repeatedly in slightly different forms, the hit rate climbs fast.

Threshold of ninety-five is deliberately high. I only want to cache things I am
confident about — a cached mediocre match is a mediocre match forever.

The version stamp is the safety net for that. It is a constant in cache.R; bump it
and every pre-existing entry stops being eligible on the next lookup, without anyone
having to remember to clear the cache after an upgrade.
:::

## 3. The postcode path — the hot path

```sql
FROM gnaf_addresses g
JOIN parsed_inputs i ON g.postcode = i.in_postcode
WHERE <number pre-filter>
  AND jaro_winkler_similarity(g.street_name, i.in_street_name) >= 0.3
```

::: {.fragment}
Two filters, both there purely to **keep the intermediate join small**:

- the **number pre-filter** (exact / in-range / suffix rule) — the gate from earlier
- a coarse **0.3 Jaro-Winkler floor** on street name, evaluated in `WHERE`, *before* scoring
:::

::: {.fragment}
Deliberately a cheap exact equi-join. Near-miss postcodes are **not retrieved here**
— that is the locality fallback's job.
:::

::: {.notes}
The zero-point-three floor is a nice illustration of the design. It is not a
correctness rule — nothing real scores below zero point three on street name. It
exists to eliminate the bulk of irrelevant rows before the more expensive full
scoring expression runs.

Cheap filter in WHERE, expensive formula only on survivors. Standard database
thinking, applied to fuzzy matching.

This path plus the compound postcode-number index is where the throughput comes
from.
:::

## 4. The state path

Same query shape, joined on `g.state = i.in_state` instead.

::: {.fragment}
For inputs with **no parseable postcode at all**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Necessarily slower and noisier — a state-wide scan instead of a postcode-blocked one.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Practical implication
If a meaningful share of your input has no postcode, that share drives your runtime.
Recovering postcodes upstream — even imperfectly — is the highest-leverage thing you
can do for performance.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Worth a moment because it changes what "make it faster" means.

If ten percent of your input has no postcode, that ten percent can be most of your
wall clock. The fix is not in gnafr — it is upstream. If you have any other field
that implies a postcode, a suburb lookup, anything, fill it in before matching.
:::

## 5. The locality fallback

Fires when the best score so far is **≤ `fallback_threshold`** (default 90) — including
inputs with no result at all — provided a locality was parsed.

Two sources of alternative postcodes, unioned:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Fuzzy locality match**

`jaro_winkler(g.locality_name, parsed) >= 0.85` against `gnaf_locality_index`
(~3,000 rows).

Finds the right postcode regardless of *how* wrong the stated one was.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Postcode offset**

Stated postcode ± 1, 2, 3.

Catches near-miss typos whose locality did not fuzzy-match — misspelt, or simply
absent.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Why ninety and not ninety-nine? Because a clean correct match typically scores
ninety-five plus, but a coincidental match — same postcode, same house number,
completely unrelated street — can still reach the low-to-mid eighties. Twenty for
postcode, partial suburb and street credit, and a lucky number match.

Ninety leaves enough margin to catch those coincidences and let the locality scan
find the real candidate, without re-triggering on matches that are already correct.

That number is a judgement call from watching real results. If your data behaves
differently, it is an argument.
:::

## 5. Locality fallback — in practice

```r
# Postcode is wildly wrong (9999). After MT -> MOUNT normalisation,
# the suburb name alone is enough to find it.
gnaf_match("77 Broadwater Road, Mt Gravatt East QLD 9999", con, min_score = 0)[
  , .(matched, match_status, total_score, score_postcode, score_suburb, address_label)]
```

::: {.fragment}
Note what cooperates here: **normalisation** (`MT` → `MOUNT`) makes the suburb
fuzzy-match; the **locality index** makes that scan cheap; the **near-miss postcode
rule** then scores what it finds.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Turn it off with `locality_fallback = FALSE` if you would rather have a fast, strict
run and handle the residue yourself.
:::

::: {.notes}
Nine-nine-nine-nine is not even a real postcode, and it still resolves. Nice demo
value.

The wider point is that the features are not independent. Normalisation earns its
keep here, three stages later, by making the fuzzy suburb match succeed. If you had
turned normalisation off for speed, this address would not resolve.
:::

## 6. Street-only fallback (opt-in)

```r
gnaf_match(addresses, con, street_only_fallback = TRUE)
```

Matches against `alias_type = 'street_only'` rows — synthetic, **number-free** address
records derived by `gnaf_build_street_aliases()`.

::: {.fragment}
Numbered inputs can never reach these rows through the ordinary paths — the number
pre-filter requires `number_first IS NULL` on the candidate side — so this path exists
precisely to give those inputs *something* once everything number-aware has failed.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Typical causes: a **brand-new subdivision** G-NAF has not published numbers for yet,
or an input that genuinely has no street number.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Normalisation]{.normalise}: turn this **on**. [Precision]{.precision}: leave it
**off** — a street-level match is a false positive for you.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the clearest single fork between the two audiences in the whole package, and
it is one argument.

For normalisation, a right-street wrong-number result is a win — you get a canonical
street, suburb, postcode and an approximate coordinate. For precision it is exactly
the kind of plausible-looking wrong answer you most want to avoid, because it scores
respectably and it is not the dwelling you asked about.

Default is off, which is the conservative choice. If you are in the normalisation
camp, switch it on and remember to check alias_type on the way out.
:::

## When nothing matches

Unmatched inputs **stay in the output** with `matched = FALSE` and a `match_status`
explaining why.

```r
results[matched == FALSE, .N, by = match_status]
#> match_status         N
#> no_candidate       412   # number gate — nothing on that street with that number
#> below_min_score     87   # candidates found, none cleared min_score
```

::: {.fragment}
Two very different problems:

- `no_candidate` → **candidate generation** failed. Lowering `min_score` will not help.
- `below_min_score` → candidates existed. Lower the threshold, or inspect components.
:::

::: {.notes}
This distinction is the most practically useful thing in the deck for day-to-day
debugging, and it is why I kept unmatched rows in the output rather than dropping
them.

No candidate means the join found nothing — usually the number gate, sometimes a
postcode not in your loaded states. Below min score means candidates existed and
none were good enough, which is a threshold conversation.

Two different fixes. Split your unmatched pile on this column before you do anything
else.
:::

## {background-color="#0b3d5c"}

### Live demo 4 — watch the cascade {.dim}

```r
# verbose = TRUE (the default) narrates every path, with timings
gnaf_match(c(
  "unit 110 120 musgrave Road red hill 4000 QLD",
  "77 broadwater rd mount gravatt east 4122",
  "10 St James Ct, Tamborine Mountain QLD 4272",
  "77 Broadwater Road, Mt Gravatt East QLD 9999",   # locality fallback
  "999 Musgrave Road, Red Hill QLD 4059"            # no_candidate
), con, max_results = 2, min_score = 20, verbose = TRUE)
```

::: {.notes}
This is the demo that makes the cascade concrete. Verbose is on by default, and it
prints which path ran, how many inputs it handled, and how long each took.

Point at the timings as they scroll: exact label and cache are milliseconds, the
postcode path is where the work is, and the fallbacks handle a handful of rows.

Then re-run the identical call so everyone sees the cache hit on the second pass.
:::

# The rest of the package {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
Core walkthrough is done. What follows is the surrounding machinery, and there is at
least one slide here for each of the workflows I know are running in this office.
:::

## Aliases — a quarter of the rows

Three independent mechanisms, all tagged by `alias_type`:

| `alias_type` | Source | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `street_only` | Derived locally by `gnaf_build_street_aliases()` | One number-free row per unique street/locality combination |
| `LOCALITY:SYN` | G-NAF's own alias tables via `gnaf_load_psv()` | A recognised alternative **suburb** name |
| `STREET:SYN` | Same | A recognised alternative **street** name |

::: {.fragment}
Plus two column pairs on *every* row, capturing G-NAF's own relationships:

- `alias_principal` / `principal_pid` — is this the canonical record, or an alias of one
- `primary_secondary` / `primary_pid` — main dwelling, or a sub-dwelling/unit
:::

::: {.notes}
The distinction that matters: street_only aliases are derived locally by dropping
the house number. They can never substitute a different name. The G-NAF synonym
tables genuinely record that this suburb is also known by that name — knowledge I
cannot derive, only load.

That is the argument for the PSV product in one line.
:::

## Controlling aliases

```r
# Everything, including synonyms and official aliases  (default)
gnaf_match(addresses, con)

# Core G-NAF and custom rows only — no synonyms at all
gnaf_match(addresses, con, include_aliases = FALSE)

# Resolve alias matches back to the canonical record
res <- gnaf_match(addresses, con, resolve_principal = TRUE)
res[!is.na(alias_type), .(address_label, principal_address_label)]
```

::: {.fragment}
`resolve_principal = TRUE` adds `principal_address_label`, `principal_longitude`,
`principal_latitude`, `principal_locality_name`, `principal_postcode` — `NA` for
non-alias matches.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Precision]{.precision}: match **with** aliases (coverage) and **resolve** to the
principal (correctness). Best of both.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the recommendation I would most like the precision people to take away.

The instinct is to switch aliases off because they feel like noise. That throws away
real coverage — a quarter of the rows — for no benefit.

The better move is to leave them on so the alias gets you the hit, then set
resolve_principal so you report the canonical record. You match on the synonym and
you output the real address.

For finer control there is an alias_types argument if you want, say, street-only but
not locality synonyms. It cannot be combined with include_aliases.
:::

## A genuine tie, broken deterministically

`6 Parkland Boulevard` and `6A Parkland Boulevard` are **separate G-NAF records**,
each with its own locality aliases.

::: {.fragment}
An input with no unit or letter suffix gives `gnaf_match()` two real, tied candidates.
It picks one **deterministically — by `address_detail_pid`, not by relevance**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So `"6 Parkland Blvd"` can resolve to `6A`. Nothing is broken; it is a genuine tie.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Precision]{.precision}: run with `max_results = 3` and check for ties in
`total_score` before you trust rank 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
I am including this because it looks like a bug the first time you see it, and
someone in this room will hit it and file it.

Determinism is the right property — the same input gives the same answer every run,
which you need for reproducibility — but PID order carries no meaning, so a tie is
broken arbitrarily even though it is broken consistently.

The defensive pattern for precision work is max_results three and check whether rank
one and rank two share a total score. If they do, that is a human decision, not a
matcher decision.
:::

## Custom addresses

```r
custom <- data.table(
  address_label = "LEVEL 2 123 CUSTOM STREET, BRISBANE QLD 4000",
  flat_type = "LEVEL", flat_number = "2",
  number_first = 123L,
  street_name = "CUSTOM", street_type = "STREET",
  locality_name = "BRISBANE", state = "QLD", postcode = 4000L,
  longitude = 153.0234, latitude = -27.4698
)

gnaf_add(con, custom)
#> Inserted 1 custom address(es). Total custom: 1.
```

Only six columns are required: `number_first`, `street_name`, `street_type`,
`locality_name`, `state`, `postcode`.

::: {.fragment}
Matched **alongside** G-NAF transparently; `source` tells you which table a result
came from. `gnaf_add(..., upsert = TRUE)` to replace; `gnaf_remove_custom(con, pids)`
to delete; `include_custom = FALSE` to ignore them for a call.
:::

::: {.notes}
This exists for the addresses G-NAF does not have or gets wrong: new subdivisions,
internal site codes, depots, known corrections.

They live in a structurally identical table in the same file, so they persist and
they participate in every matching path. The source column is your audit trail —
always keep it in anything you hand on, so a reviewer can see the match came from
your local table rather than the national dataset.
:::

## Bulk matching

```r
dt_in   <- fread("C:/data/my_addresses.csv")
results <- gnaf_match(dt_in$address_string, con, max_results = 1, min_score = 60)

dt_in[, input_id := .I]
dt_out <- results[dt_in, on = "input_id"]
```

**Pass the whole vector in one call.** Internally:

1. **Parse once** — unique normalised inputs parsed with vectorised regex, expanded back
2. **Deduplicate signatures** — equivalent parsed inputs enter DuckDB only once
3. **Exact component stage** — postcode, street name, number branches before any fuzzy work
4. **Fuzzy fallback** — only weak or unmatched inputs go wider
5. **Narrow ranking** — score and rank on PIDs, fetch wide columns only for top rows

::: {.notes}
The instruction that matters is the first line: one call, whole vector. If you
lapply over rows you lose every one of those five optimisations, and it will be
orders of magnitude slower.

Step two is worth dwelling on for anyone with administrative data. Duplicate
addresses collapse before they reach the database, so a hundred thousand rows
containing twenty thousand distinct addresses costs about twenty thousand rows of
work.

Step five is a classic late-materialisation trick: rank on the narrow columns, join
back for the wide ones only on the rows that survived.
:::

## Performance

| Input size | Estimated time |
|---|---|
| 1,000 | < 1 second |
| 10,000 | 2–5 seconds |
| 100,000 | 15–45 seconds |
| 500,000 | 2–5 minutes (chunk recommended) |

<p class="dim">Laptop with SSD, ~3M G-NAF records (QLD). Varies with CPU, postcode spread, and the share of inputs with no postcode.</p>

::: {.fragment}
```r
chunk_size <- 50000L
ids    <- seq_len(nrow(dt_in))
chunks <- split(ids, ceiling(ids / chunk_size))

results <- rbindlist(lapply(chunks, function(idx)
  gnaf_match(dt_in$address_string[idx], con, max_results = 1)))
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Be honest that these are estimates from my machine, not a benchmark suite. The
distribution of your input matters more than the row count.

The specific pathology to know: if a hundred thousand addresses all share one
postcode and their numbers do not parse, the broad fallback join is a hundred
thousand times two thousand G-NAF records — two hundred million pairs. Peak memory,
not CPU, is what bites.

Chunking is the pressure valve. Above roughly five hundred thousand rows, or
anything with a heavy postcode concentration, chunk it.
:::

## Round-trip benchmarking

`benchmark_match.R` samples real records, perturbs them, and measures recovery:

```r
inputs  <- address_perturb_sample(source_rows, n = 100000, seed = 42, max_changes = 2L)
matches <- gnaf_match(inputs$simulated_address, con, cache = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
```

Reports `inputs_per_second`, `matched_rate`, `exact_pid_rate`, and `resolved_pid_rate`.

::: {.fragment}
Because the inputs were **generated from known PIDs**, this measures **accuracy**, not
just throughput — you know the right answer.
:::

::: {.fragment}
`resolved_pid_rate` counts an alias match as correct once resolved to its principal —
which is the number that matters if you are using `resolve_principal = TRUE`.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is how I evaluate changes to the parser or the weights, and I would recommend
the same approach if you are comparing gnafr against whatever you use now.

It is a fair-ish test with one honest caveat: the perturbations are my model of
messiness, not your data's actual messiness. If you have a hand-labelled set, that
beats this. If you do not, this is a repeatable regression check that costs nothing
to run.

The seed makes it reproducible, so a change in the rate is a change in the code, not
in the sample.
:::

## Synthetic messy addresses

```r
synthetic <- address_perturb_sample(
  sample_gnaf(con, n = 100), n = 5, seed = 42, max_changes = 2L
)
synthetic[, .(address_label, simulated_address, perturbations)]
```

Perturbations: typos, abbreviation swaps, dropped components. `max_changes` caps how
many per address; `keep_original = TRUE` (default) keeps the clean label alongside.

::: {.fragment}
Round-trip it straight back through `gnaf_match()` — a repeatable regression check
after changing weights or parser logic, with no hand-labelling required.
:::

::: {.notes}
Useful beyond gnafr, incidentally. If you are evaluating any address matcher, this
gives you a labelled test set out of data you already have.

The perturbations column tells you exactly what was done to each address, so when
something fails to recover you can see whether it was the typo, the dropped suburb,
or the abbreviation swap that broke it.
:::

## Spatial helpers

```r
sa2     <- read_shapefile("C:/temp/sa2/SA2_2021_AUST_GDA2020.shp")
sa2_qld <- subset_shapefile(sa2, var = "STE_NAME21", values = "Queensland")

geo <- spatial_lookup(
  matched[matched == TRUE], sa2_qld,
  lat = "latitude", lon = "longitude",
  return_cols = c("SA2_CODE21", "SA2_NAME21")
)

plot_boundaries_heatmap(sa2_qld, points_dt = geo, bins = 200)
plot_boundaries_heatmap(sa2_qld, points_dt = geo, use_leaflet = TRUE)
```

::: {.fragment}
`spatial_lookup()` chunks points (`chunk_size`, default 100,000) to bound memory, and
supports `multiple = "all"` for overlapping polygons.
:::

::: {.notes}
These exist to close the loop, not to replace your GIS tooling. If you already have
an sf workflow you are happy with, use it — the coordinates are just columns in a
data.table.

The chunking matters on big batches. A point-in-polygon join over a million points
and a fine polygon set will happily exhaust memory if you do it in one go.

The heatmap is genuinely useful as a QA step: match density that does not look like
population density usually means something went wrong upstream.
:::

## The Shiny geocoder

```r
gnaf_app(db_path = "C:/temp/gnaf.duckdb")
gnaf_app(con = con)                    # reuse an open connection
app <- gnaf_app(con = con, run = FALSE)  # embed in a larger app
```

Paste one address per line. Runs the same `gnaf_match()` — nothing in the app does its
own matching.

::: {.fragment}
Adds two review-oriented diagnostics on top of the usual columns: full-string
**Jaro-Winkler** and **Jaccard** similarity between the raw input and the matched
`address_label`, with gradient highlighting.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A structurally perfect match that is *textually* distant from the input is a signal
the parse went down an unexpected path — visible at a glance.
:::

::: {.notes}
The app is for ad hoc lookups and for manual review, not for volume.

The two extra similarity columns are the interesting part. The structured score
tells you the components agreed. The full-string similarity tells you whether the
result still looks like what the user typed. When those two disagree — high
structured score, low lexical similarity — it is nearly always worth a human look.

That combination is a decent triage rule for a review queue even outside the app.
:::

## The match cache, day to day

```r
gnaf_cache_status(con)                       # how many entries, how old
gnaf_cache_history(con, by = "day")          # growth and score distribution
gnaf_cache_sample(con, n = 10)               # eyeball what is in there
gnaf_cache_rollback(con, after = "2026-06-05 14:00:00")
gnaf_cache_clear(con)
```

::: {.fragment}
- **Slower than expected?** Check `gnaf_cache_status()` first — an empty cache means everything went through the full pipeline
- **`avg_score` dropped for a day?** Usually harder input, not a regression
- **Bad batch?** `rollback` re-matches exactly that window and keeps everything else
:::

::: {.notes}
Rollback over clear, wherever you can scope it. Clearing throws away everything the
cache has learned, and rebuilding it costs a full pass over your input.

The history function is a quiet monitoring tool. If the average cached score drops
sharply on a given day, go and look at what you loaded that day. It is usually a
messier source, occasionally a genuine upstream data problem — either way you want to
know.

And remember: custom weights mean these tables stay empty. That is expected.
:::

# Choosing your settings {background-color="#12405c"}

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff slide for the thread I started at the beginning. If people
remember nothing else after the demo, I want them to leave with the right argument
set for their team.
:::

## Two recipes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### [High precision]{.precision}

```r
gnaf_match(
  addresses, con,
  max_results          = 3,
  min_score            = 90,
  street_only_fallback = FALSE,
  include_aliases      = TRUE,
  resolve_principal    = TRUE,
  weights = list(
    postcode = 18, suburb = 12,
    street_name = 35, street_type = 8,
    number = 17, flat = 10
  )
)
```

Then: check ties, filter `score_flat`, review `score_number < 10`.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
### [Normalisation]{.normalise}

```r
gnaf_match(
  addresses, con,
  max_results          = 1,
  min_score            = 40,
  street_only_fallback = TRUE,
  include_aliases      = TRUE,
  resolve_principal    = TRUE
)
```

Then: take `address_label` as your canonical string, keep `alias_type` and
`total_score` as caveat columns.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Talk through the differences rather than reading the code.

Precision: three results so you can see ties. Ninety cutoff. Street-only off,
because a street-level match is a false positive for you. Number and flat weighted
up, street name and postcode down to make room. Aliases on for coverage, resolved to
the principal for correctness.

Normalisation: one result, forty cutoff, street-only on. You want an answer for
nearly everything, and a right-street wrong-number answer is still useful. Take
address_label as your canonical string and carry the score and alias type through as
caveats.

Both are the same engine and the same database file.
:::

## One run can serve both

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '15px'}}}%%
flowchart LR
  A["Your addresses"] --> B["gnaf_match(<br/>min_score = 0,<br/>max_results = 3,<br/>street_only_fallback = TRUE)"]
  B --> C[("All candidates<br/>with full score<br/>breakdown")]
  C --> D["total_score >= 90<br/>score_flat == 5<br/>no ties"]
  C --> E["rank 1, any score<br/>keep alias_type<br/>keep address_label"]
  D --> F["Precision consumers"]
  E --> G["Normalisation consumers"]
```

::: {.fragment}
Match **once**, permissively. Keep every candidate and every component. Let each
downstream consumer apply its own bar — filtering is free, re-matching is not.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the architectural suggestion I would actually make to this office.

Rather than each area running its own matcher with its own settings, run one
permissive pass, store the full candidate set with the score breakdown, and let each
team filter. Filtering is a data.table subset. Re-matching is minutes to hours.

It also means the awkward conversations — is a street-level match acceptable, is a
tie a match — happen in explicit filter code that someone can read and review,
rather than being buried in whatever arguments a script happened to use.
:::

## What gnafr is not

- **Not a geocoder for non-Australian addresses** — the parser is built around Australian conventions
- **Not a PO Box resolver** — no street component to anchor on
- **Not a full GIS toolkit** — the `sf`/`leaflet` helpers make results usable, not a replacement for real spatial tooling
- **Not a source of truth** — it matches against whatever G-NAF release you loaded

::: {.fragment}
It is also **version 0.1.0** and in active development. The API for `gnaf_match()` has
been stable; the internals have not.
:::

::: {.notes}
Closing honestly matters more than closing strongly.

The last point is the important one for anyone considering this for production: it
is early, it is one maintainer, and the internals move. The mitigations are that the
test suite covers parse, score and match, and that the database file is just DuckDB
— if the package disappeared tomorrow, your data is still queryable with SQL.

Do not let me talk anyone into ripping out something that works. The interesting
question is whether this is better for the specific thing you are struggling with.
:::

## Where to get it

```r
install.packages(c("data.table", "DBI", "duckdb", "stringdist"))
install.packages(c("shiny", "reactable"))   # for gnaf_app()

devtools::install_github("KyleHaynes/gnafr")
```

- **Docs:** [kylehaynes.github.io/gnafr](https://kylehaynes.github.io/gnafr) — About, Quick guide, Theory, Building a good lookup table, Function reference, Alias matching, Troubleshooting
- **G-NAF download:** [geoscape.com.au/data/g-naf](https://geoscape.com.au/data/g-naf/) — free and open
- **Source:** `R/parse.R`, `R/score.R`, `R/match.R` are the three worth reading

::: {.notes}
The theory chapter in the docs is essentially this deck with the code chunks
actually executed, so it is the right thing to send anyone who missed today.

The alias chapter is the one that runs against a real full-size database rather than
a synthetic one, so its numbers are real.
:::
